lead: An operational transconductance amplifier (OTA) takes a voltage difference at its input and delivers a current at its output. The ratio of the two is the transconductance Gm, in siemens, that is, amperes per volt. Gm is not fixed: an external bias current IBIAS sets it, so the same chip can be made more or less sensitive while it runs. OTAs are the building block of tunable continuous-time filters, variable-gain amplifiers and sine-wave oscillators inside integrated circuits.
prereq: You need: the differential pair (5.1), the current mirror (5.3) and the active-load CMOS stage (5.4).

sections.h3: A voltage in, a current out

blocks.text: The OTA symbol is a triangle like an op-amp's, with one extra terminal: the bias input. One line describes its job.

blocks.where: Iout is the output current in A; Gm is the transconductance in A/V (siemens); v₊ and v₋ are the voltages at the two inputs, both in V; vid is their difference in V.

blocks.text: The output is a current source. A current source has a very high output resistance Rout, often hundreds of kilohms, so the output current barely changes when the voltage at the output node changes. Connect a resistor R from the output to ground and that current produces a voltage Gm × vid × R. Connect a capacitor C instead and the current charges it, so the output voltage becomes an integral of vid.

An op-amp is different. It has a voltage output, an output resistance of a few ohms or less, and enough open-loop gain that feedback fixes the closed-loop gain as a ratio of two resistors. An OTA has no such buffer: the voltage at its output is decided by whatever circuit you attach, and its gain Gm × R changes whenever the bias current changes.

sections.h3: Setting Gm with the bias current

blocks.text: Take the CMOS differential pair with a tail current source IBIAS and a current-mirror load. At vid = 0 the tail current splits equally, so each transistor carries ID = IBIAS/2 and sits at an overdrive VOV = VGS − VTH. The small-signal transconductance of one transistor is gm = 2ID/VOV = √(2k′(W/L)ID). A differential input vid shifts current from one side to the other; the difference of the two drain currents is the output current, Iout = Gm × vid, where Gm is the expression below.

blocks.where: Gm is the transconductance in A/V; IBIAS is the tail bias current in A; VOV = VGS − VTH is the quiescent overdrive in V; ID = IBIAS/2 is the drain current of each device in A; k′ = µCox is the process transconductance parameter in A/V²; W/L is the aspect ratio, dimensionless.

blocks.text: The last form is the tuning knob. Gm rises as the square root of IBIAS, so quadrupling the bias current only doubles Gm. The path stays biased with a balanced output and the input common-mode level can stay fixed, but ID and VOV do move with IBIAS: VOV changes as √IBIAS.

A BJT pair behaves differently. Its transconductance is IC/VT = IBIAS/(2VT), directly proportional to the bias current, and its transfer curve is Iout = IBIAS × tanh(vid/(2VT)), with VT ≈ 26 mV at room temperature.

sections.h3: Linear range, and where OTAs are used

blocks.text: The formula Iout = Gm × vid is a small-signal result. The pair is close to linear only for |vid| well below VOV — a few tens of millivolts for a few percent error of slope. At |vid| = VOV the slope Gm has already fallen by about 40 percent. The current saturates at |vid| = √2 × VOV, where one transistor takes the whole tail current. For a BJT pair the same flattening starts at about ±VT, only ±26 mV.

items: Gm-C filters: in a Gm-C filter each resistor is replaced by an OTA, the capacitor stays, and the cut-off frequency becomes Gm/C, which moves with IBIAS.
Variable-gain amplifiers: the gain Gm × R is set electrically, with no switched resistors.
Oscillators and waveform generators: an OTA feeding a capacitor makes an integrator whose time constant can be trimmed.
On-chip resistors: a precise resistor is hard to build in CMOS, so an OTA with feedback emulates one whose value is 1/Gm.

blocks.text: Some OTAs add an output buffer inside the package, so the part has a current-mode core and a voltage output. Without that buffer an OTA must drive a virtual ground or a high-impedance node, never a heavy load.

figure.caption: The bias current sets Gm, the input difference drives the output current, and the high output resistance keeps the output behaving as a current source rather than a voltage source.

spec.title: OTA as a tunable transconductor
spec.aria: Block diagram: bias current IBIAS sets the transconductance Gm, the input difference vid controls the output current Iout, and the output has high resistance so it behaves as a current source.

examples.question: A simple CMOS OTA uses a differential pair with k′ = 100 µA/V², W/L = 25 and a tail bias current IBIAS = 100 µA. (a) Find the overdrive VOV of each device. (b) Find Gm. (c) Find the output current for vid = 10 mV. (d) State the limit of the linear range.
steps: Each device carries half the tail current: ID = IBIAS/2 = 100 µA / 2 = 50 µA.
Square-law overdrive: VOV = √(2ID/(k′(W/L))) = √(2 × 50 µA / (100 µA/V² × 25)) = √(100 µA / 2500 µA/V²) = √0.04 V² = 0.2 V.
Transconductance from the operating point: Gm = 2ID/VOV = 2 × 50 µA / 0.2 V = 100 µA / 0.2 V = 5 × 10⁻⁴ A/V = 0.5 mS.
Cross-check with the bias form: Gm = IBIAS/VOV = 100 µA / 0.2 V = 5 × 10⁻⁴ A/V. Same value, so the arithmetic is consistent.
Cross-check with the process form: Gm = √(2k′(W/L)ID) = √(2 × 100 µA/V² × 25 × 50 µA) = √(2.5 × 10⁻⁷ A²) = 5 × 10⁻⁴ A/V. Same again.
Output current: Iout = Gm × vid = 5 × 10⁻⁴ A/V × 10 × 10⁻³ V = 5 × 10⁻⁶ A = 5 µA.
This is 5 µA out of a 100 µA tail current, only 5 percent of the ±100 µA limit, so the small-signal formula is valid here.

Linear range: close to linear only for |vid| well below VOV — a few tens of millivolts for a few percent slope error. At |vid| = VOV = 0.2 V the slope has already fallen by about 40 percent. The current saturates at |vid| = √2 × 0.2 V = 0.283 V, where one device carries the whole tail current.
examples.answer: VOV = 0.2 V, Gm = 0.5 mS, Iout = 5 µA for vid = 10 mV. The pair is linear only well below 0.2 V: at |vid| = 0.2 V the slope has fallen by about 40 percent, and the current saturates near ±0.283 V.
examples.check:
import math
kprime = 100e-6
wl = 25.0
ibias = 100e-6
vid = 10e-3
idq = ibias / 2
vov = math.sqrt(2 * idq / (kprime * wl))
gm = 2 * idq / vov
iout = gm * vid
vlim = math.sqrt(2) * vov
print(vov)
print(gm)
print(iout)
print(vlim)

traps: Calling Gm a voltage gain. Gm is a conductance in A/V; a voltage gain is dimensionless. The OTA's voltage gain is Gm × R and depends on the load you attach.
Using Iout = Gm × vid outside the linear range. The output current cannot exceed ±IBIAS, and the slope collapses near |vid| = √2 × VOV.
Forgetting that Gm moves with IBIAS. In a Gm-C filter, changing the bias current changes the cut-off frequency, the gain and the distortion together.
Assuming the OTA can drive any load. With no buffer its output resistance is very high, so a heavy resistive load converts the current into a voltage and also destroys the intended transconductance.
Taking Iout as the drain current of one transistor. It is the difference of the two drain currents, which is why the bias current cancels and the common-mode input is rejected.

quiz.q: Define transconductance and give its unit.
quiz.a: Transconductance is the ratio of output current to input voltage difference, Gm = Iout/vid. Its unit is the siemens, S = A/V.

quiz.q: State two ways an OTA differs from a voltage op-amp.
quiz.a: The OTA output is a current with very high output resistance and no buffer; the op-amp output is a voltage with very low output resistance. The OTA's transconductance is small and set by an external bias current; the op-amp's open-loop gain is large and fixed.

quiz.q: Why does the basic OTA deliberately avoid an output buffer?
quiz.a: A buffer would lower the output resistance, so the output current would start to depend on the output voltage and the device would no longer behave as a current source. Buffers are added only in variants meant to drive loads directly.

quiz.q: An OTA has Gm = 0.4 mS and VOV = 0.25 V. Find Iout for vid = 20 mV and say whether the small-signal formula is valid.
quiz.a: Iout = Gm × vid = 0.4 × 10⁻³ A/V × 20 × 10⁻³ V = 8 × 10⁻⁶ A = 8 µA. Here |vid| = 20 mV is well below VOV = 0.25 V, so the pair is inside the linear range and the formula holds.

quiz.q: The bias current of a CMOS OTA is raised from 50 µA to 200 µA. By what factor does Gm change?
quiz.a: For a CMOS pair Gm = √(k′(W/L)IBIAS), so Gm is proportional to √IBIAS. The ratio is √(200/50) = √4 = 2, so Gm doubles.

quiz.q: Explain why Gm falls when vid becomes large.
quiz.a: As vid grows, one device takes more of the tail current and the other less. The extra current available on the weaker side shrinks, so the incremental change in the difference current for a further increase in vid gets smaller. At |vid| = √2 × VOV one device takes the whole tail and the other is cut off; the current cannot rise further, so the slope dIout/dvid becomes zero.

quiz.q: Why is a tunable OTA preferred over a diffused resistor in an integrated continuous-time filter?
quiz.a: An integrated resistor has a large process spread (its value can differ widely from chip to chip) and cannot be adjusted after fabrication, and its value drifts with temperature. In an OTA-C filter the equivalent resistance is 1/Gm, set by a bias current, so the cut-off frequency Gm/C can be trimmed on the bench or by a tuning loop, and several filters on one chip can track each other.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical OTA design is largely a fight against the small linear range: source-degenerated pairs, adaptive biasing and class-AB input stages stretch the ±VOV limit to a volt or more. These linearised OTAs are what make continuous-time Gm-C filters in CMOS radios possible, where the cut-off frequency has to be trimmed after manufacture. The same tunable transconductor also appears inside on-chip automatic gain control loops. Search for 'linearised OTA', 'Gm-C filter tuning' and 'bulk-driven OTA' to go further.
